subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage: The daycare door in Helsinki opened at four and Kaito, nineteen months old, was sitting on the mat with a wooden puzzle. He looked up. Sami stood in the doorway, still in his cycling jacket. Kaito's whole face opened into a wide smile, cheeks round, eyes crinkled, and he dropped the puzzle piece and ran with his arms out. “Hello, you,” said Sami, scooping him up. Kaito patted his father's cheek and kept smiling, then pointed back at the puzzle to show him.

qa.q: Where did Sami pick up Kaito?
qa.a: At the daycare in Helsinki, at four o'clock.

qa.q: What does Kaito's smile tell you about how he feels toward Sami?
qa.a: It suggests delight and closeness, since he smiled, dropped the piece and ran straight to him. It is a natural greeting for his age rather than a hidden plan.

qa.q: What could Sami do next to keep the connection going?
qa.a: He could look at the puzzle with Kaito, smile back and say what he sees, giving the happy moment some words. 😊

qa.q: How might the daycare staff see Kaito's greeting?
qa.a: They may see a child who is securely attached and glad to be reunited, which tells them he feels safe with his father.

grounding: A toddler beams at a familiar caregiver, showing delight and attachment without any hidden purpose.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage: Our lane's little Pallavi, about two, sits on her doorstep every evening waiting. I watch from my window. When her father Uday rounds the corner on his bicycle, she beams, kicks both feet and calls “Papa!” She does it the same way for her grandfather and, I noticed, for the milk-delivery man once, who happened to wave. I can't tell exactly what she thinks. To me it looks like plain gladness at a friendly, familiar face, nothing sly about it.

qa.q: Where does Pallavi sit each evening?
qa.a: On her doorstep, waiting for her father to come around the corner.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Pallavi's beam means, and what is left uncertain?
qa.a: The narrator thinks it is plain gladness at a friendly, familiar face, seen in the kicking feet and the call of “Papa”. She admits she cannot know exactly what Pallavi is thinking.

qa.q: What could Uday do when he sees the smile?
qa.a: He could get off the bicycle, smile back and greet her by name so the happy moment is shared. 😊

qa.q: What might the milk-delivery man feel when Pallavi beams at him?
qa.a: He may feel pleasantly surprised and welcomed, since a toddler's smile is easy to take as a small greeting even from a passer-by.

grounding: A toddler beams at familiar people as an open social signal of delight, seen by a neighbour who cannot be sure of her thoughts.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage:
Tuesday morning: Saurabh came home from his night shift. Yamini, still in her sleep suit, saw him at the door and beamed, her whole face lit up, arms flapping.
Friday: Saurabh was away at a training. When his voice came from the video call, Yamini beamed at the screen and patted it.
Next Monday: he walked in with his bag. Nani said, "Smiling like that, she wants a sweet from you."
Saurabh laughed and lifted Yamini. "No, Mummy-ji. She's just glad I'm back."

qa.q: Where was Saurabh on Friday?
qa.a: He was away at a training, and Yamini heard his voice on a video call.

qa.q: What does Yamini's beaming smile suggest she felt each time?
qa.a: Delight and a warm bond with Saurabh, shown by her lit-up face and flapping arms whenever she saw or heard him; it is joy at a familiar person, not a plan to get something.

qa.q: How could Saurabh keep that connection strong on the days he is away?
qa.a: He could keep up the calls and greet her warmly when he returns, so she keeps getting a smile back.

qa.q: Why might Nani read the smile differently from Saurabh?
qa.a: Nani may be used to older children who smile to get treats, while Saurabh sees a toddler's simple happiness at his return.

grounding: Across several days a toddler beams at a familiar caregiver, showing delight and attachment rather than any plan.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage:
The doorbell rang in the Kolkata flat, and Vasudha from next door came in with her cloth bag. Bidisha, in her high chair, beamed so wide her eyes crinkled, and she drummed her feet on the tray.
"She never smiles like that at me in the morning," her Ma said, half joking. "Maybe she knows you bring biscuits."
Vasudha shook her head. "Look, the bag is closed. She's smiling at me, not the biscuits." Bidisha reached out both hands.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do with her feet when Vasudha came in?
qa.a: She drummed her feet on the tray of her high chair.

qa.q: What might Bidisha's crinkle-eyed smile show about her feelings?
qa.a: Joy and fondness at seeing a familiar person, shown by reaching out both hands even though the bag was closed; it is unlikely she was hoping for biscuits.

qa.q: What could Ma do if she feels a little left out?
qa.a: She could notice her own warm moments with Bidisha too, and enjoy that Bidisha is attached to more than one caring adult.

qa.q: How does Ma see the big smile?
qa.a: Ma feels a small pang and half suspects the smile is about biscuits, while Vasudha takes it as simple gladness.

grounding: A toddler beams at a familiar neighbour, a social smile of delight rather than a calculated one.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage:
"Is he always this quiet?" asked Yogesh's Papa at the creche door.
"Mostly calm," said Dilnaz, the teacher. "He smiled at the fish tank today."
"Just the fish tank?"
"Wait." Dilnaz stepped aside. Yogesh looked up from the rug, saw his Papa and beamed, a huge gummy grin. He toddled over at full speed.
"There. That smile is only for you."
Papa laughed. "I was worried he forgets me all day."
"He doesn't. He saves it."

qa.q: What did Yogesh smile at earlier in the day?
qa.a: He smiled at the fish tank.

qa.q: What was Papa worried about before Yogesh saw him?
qa.a: Papa was worried that Yogesh forgets him during the day at the creche; the big grin left him relieved and happy.

qa.q: How could Dilnaz help other parents who feel the same worry?
qa.a: She could let them see their child's greeting at pick-up and share small moments from the day, as she did with Yogesh's Papa.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when Yogesh beams at his Papa?
qa.a: She probably feels warm and glad, because the smile shows Yogesh's bond with his father. 🙂

grounding: A toddler's beaming smile at a familiar parent at pick-up, showing delight and attachment.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. From Rafiq, room lead.
Mridul had a lovely morning. When I came into the room with the snack tray, he dropped his blocks and beamed at me, his whole face crinkled, arms flapping 🙂.
At pickup he did the same for his Dadi, then hid his face in her shoulder and peeped out, still grinning.
A new helper asked if he was “buttering us up.” I said no, that's simply him being glad to see people he knows.
I smiled back each time and told his Dadi about it.

qa.q: What did Mridul drop when Rafiq came in with the snack tray?
qa.a: He dropped his blocks.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he beamed at Rafiq and his Dadi?
qa.a: He was feeling happy and delighted to see familiar people; the crinkled face and flapping arms show joy and closeness, not a plan.

qa.q: How could the new helper respond to Mridul's beaming next time?
qa.a: The helper could simply smile back and talk to him, treating the beam as a warm hello rather than a trick.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul's Dadi to get that beam at pickup?
qa.a: She probably feels loved and reassured that he is attached to her, and hearing about his morning adds to that.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler beaming at familiar caregivers out of delight and attachment, not to hide or plan anything.
